extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, IPR petitioners, patent owners, PTO examiners and adjudicators, and appellate judges
extracted.subtask_description: Standards governing whether and how applicant-admitted prior art (AAPA) in a challenged patent may be used in an inter partes review (IPR), including the meaning of 35 U.S.C. § 311(b)'s phrase "prior art consisting of patents or printed publications," permissible uses of AAPA as evidence, and procedural requirements for IPR petitions and Board decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: § 311(b) 'patents or printed publications' must themselves be prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: The language of § 311(b) limits “the basis” of any “ground” in an inter partes review to “prior art consisting of patents or printed publications.” The patents or printed publications that form the basis of a ground must themselves be prior art to the challenged patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This interpretation excludes descriptions of the prior art contained in the challenged patent from being the § 311(b) basis. The court cites Return Mail, Regents of the Univ. of Minn., In re Lonardo, and related precedent to support reading the phrase to refer to document-based prior art (i.e., documents that themselves are prior art).

rubrics_metrics.name: AAPA may not form the 'basis' of an IPR ground (cannot be the sole basis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant-admitted prior art (AAPA) contained in the challenged patent does not constitute 'prior art consisting of patents or printed publications' under § 311(b) and therefore may not form the basis of a ground in an inter partes review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A petition that relies solely on AAPA without also relying on a prior-art patent or printed publication is impermissible. The court vacated the Board's decision and remanded for the Board to determine whether the petitioner nonetheless relied on prior-art patents/printed publications (e.g., Majcherczak) as the basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: AAPA can be used as evidence of the skilled artisan's general knowledge (limited purposes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although AAPA cannot be the § 311(b) basis of a ground, admissions in the specification of the challenged patent may be relied upon in IPR proceedings as evidence of what a person of ordinary skill in the art (POSA) would have known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permissible uses include furnishing a motivation to combine references, supplying a missing claim limitation, and establishing background knowledge. The court cites Koninklijke Philips, PharmaStem, Randal Manufacturing, McCoy, and other precedent describing these limited evidentiary uses. Such evidence is not a § 311(b) document-basis but may support an obviousness determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petitioners may submit non‑prior‑art supporting evidence (affidavits, expert opinions, supplemental info)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory provisions allow petitioners to rely on evidence beyond prior-art documents in an IPR, such as affidavits, declarations, and expert opinions, and permit submission of supplemental information after filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited statutes include 35 U.S.C. §§ 312(a)(3)(B) (affidavits/declarations), 314(a) (Director considers information presented in the petition), and 316(a)(3) (procedures for supplemental submissions). Case law (e.g., Yeda) supports reliance on non-prior-art documents for limited purposes in IPRs. However, such evidence cannot substitute for the § 311(b) requirement that the basis be prior-art patents/printed publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial petition must identify supporting evidence with particularity (timeliness and specificity requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The initial IPR petition must identify with particularity the evidence that supports the grounds for the challenge to each claim; petitioners must adhere to this requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court quotes Intelligent Bio‑Sys.: 'It is of the utmost importance that petitioners in IPR proceedings adhere to the requirement that the initial petition identify with particularity the evidence...' New theories or motivations to combine raised for the first time on reply may be deemed untimely and disregarded (see Henny Penny; Apple’s hysteresis theory was untimely).

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissions in a patent specification are binding on the patentee for anticipation/obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements in a patent that something is in the prior art (AAPA) are binding on the applicant/patentee for determinations of anticipation and obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court references PharmaStem and Constant v. AMD to show that a patentee’s own characterization of prior art in the specification can be treated as an admission and relied upon in later invalidity analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation to combine requirement and evidentiary standard
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish obviousness, a petitioner must show a motivation to combine prior-art references and that a skilled artisan would have been motivated to make the combination; the showing must be timely and supported by substantial evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board and courts will not credit an asserted motivation to combine if it was not timely presented in the petition or if it lacks explanatory support as to why a POSA would have made the combination (see Intelligent Bio‑Sys; Henny Penny; discussion of Apple’s failure to show motivation to combine Doyle and Steinacker).

rubrics_metrics.name: Director/PTO guidance and remand practice
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Board's treatment of AAPA and § 311(b) is unclear or involved, the court may remand for the Board to apply Director guidance and to determine in the first instance whether the petitioner relied on prior-art patents/printed publications as the basis of its ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PTO’s Guidance (Treatment of Statements of the Applicant in the Challenged Patent in IPRs Under § 311(b)) agrees AAPA is not itself § 311(b) prior art but permits AAPA as evidence of general knowledge; the court remanded for the Board to determine whether the petitioner's § 103 challenge nonetheless rests on proper prior-art documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative/policy purpose limiting 'basis' to printed documents (to streamline proceedings)
rubrics_metrics.description: The restriction in § 311(b) to prior-art patents or printed publications reflects a congressional purpose to create a streamlined administrative proceeding that avoids fact-intensive inquiries (e.g., commercial sales, public uses) and focuses on documentary prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court explains that holding patentees to descriptions in their own specifications does not implicate the fact-intensive inquiries Congress sought to avoid (citing Quad Environmental Techs. and legislative history), which supports allowing AAPA only as a limited evidentiary matter rather than as the basis of an IPR ground.
